People from more than 30 countries are missing after the flash floods in Nepal and China

A glacier collapse in Tibet triggered catastrophic flash flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border, resulting in significant casualties and missing persons. Authorities in both countries reported over 160 deaths and more than 1,300 people missing as of Thursday. Many of the missing were foreigners in the area for trekking or a pilgrimage to a sacred Hindu site. The number of missing may vary due to differences in data collection, reporting, and verification. Nepal Police reported at least 165 dead and 826 missing, while China State media reported at least three deaths and 558 missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The U.S. State Department confirmed about 90 Americans are missing, though no confirmed deaths of U.S. citizens have been reported. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it will send $1.2 million in emergency funding to the Nepal Red Cross.

Where the accounts differ

Associated Press and Al Jazeera both reported that Nepal Police said 826 people were missing, including 113 Nepali tourists, 85 security personnel, and 161 residents from Rasuwa district. UPI and NPR reported that Nepal Tourism Board later said 517 foreigners were missing, while Al Jazeera and NPR stated that Nepal said 600 foreign tourists were missing. UPI reported that China said 260 of the 558 missing were foreigners, while Al Jazeera and NPR reported that China said 260 foreign nationals were missing in Tibet. UPI and NPR also reported that India said 133 Indians were missing on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, while Al Jazeera and Associated Press reported that India said 179 of those missing were from India. UPI and NPR reported that the U.S. said 65 of the missing were from the United States, while Al Jazeera and Associated Press reported that the U.S. said 65 of the missing were from the United States. UPI and NPR reported that Australia said 34 citizens were missing, while Al Jazeera and Associated Press reported that Australia said 34 citizens were missing.

Sources Associated Press · UPI · BBC · The Guardian · NPR · Al Jazeera

Trump's mail-voting rules face legal battles as courts weigh their legality

A federal judge in Boston has issued conflicting rulings on the legality of President Trump's executive order aimed at tightening mail-in voting rules ahead of the midterm elections. On Wednesday, Judge Indira Talwani lifted a nationwide block on the Postal Service's new requirements for mail ballots, allowing the agency to proceed with implementing the rule. However, on Thursday, she issued a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the rule for 14 days, citing concerns over voter disenfranchisement. The judge argued that the rule, which requires states to submit voter lists and use standardized ballot envelopes, risks preventing voters from casting ballots by mail. The Supreme Court had previously allowed the rule to move forward, but the court did not rule on its legality.

The White House has defended the rule as a necessary measure to ensure election security, with White House spokesperson Lauren Bis calling it "commonsense election integrity measures." The rule, which was finalized by the Postal Service in late August, requires states to submit voter information through a federal portal and use barcoded envelopes for ballots. Critics, including Democratic-led states and voting rights groups, argue the rule oversteps federal authority and could suppress voter turnout.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that a federal judge lifted a nationwide block on the Postal Service's rule, while The New York Post and Washington Examiner state that the same judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the rule. NPR and FOX News also note the judge issued a temporary restraining order, but NPR adds that the judge reestablished a nationwide block she had previously put on USPS' efforts. The Daily Wire states that the Supreme Court allowed the rule to move forward, while the New York Post and Washington Examiner clarify that the court only addressed a procedural issue and did not rule on the rule's legality.

Sources Axios · The Daily Wire · New York Post · NPR · Washington Examiner · FOX News

Meta agrees to $18 billion settlement with states over child safety claims

Meta has reached a settlement with 52 U.S. states, U.S. territories, and Washington, D.C., agreeing to pay up to $18 billion to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. The agreement includes measures such as two-hour daily time limits for under-18 users, nighttime access restrictions, and parental controls. The company also urged rival platforms like YouTube and TikTok to adopt similar policies. The settlement ends a federal trial that could have resulted in billions in damages for Meta.

The settlement requires Meta to implement changes to its platforms, including limiting notifications for children during school hours, blocking access from midnight to 6 a.m., and offering a non-personalized feed as an option. Meta did not admit wrongdoing and stated that its existing protections for young users are sufficient. The agreement also includes provisions for an independent auditor to assess compliance with the terms.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that whistleblower Arturo Béjar criticized the settlement as insufficient, arguing it does not address algorithmic design choices that make Meta’s platforms addictive. The Daily Wire notes that the settlement includes a $17.1 billion figure, while other accounts cite $18 billion. Axios states the settlement is $16.7 billion, with $5 billion contingent on TikTok and YouTube joining. Fox Business mentions a $18 billion settlement, while the Daily Wire and BBC report $18 billion. The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention that Meta did not admit wrongdoing, while Axios and Fox Business note that the company did not accept any wrongdoing.

Sources BBC · The Guardian · Mother Jones · Axios · Fox Business · The Daily Wire

Dolly Parton Dies At 80 After Battle With Cancer; Funeral Plans Revealed

Dolly Parton died at 80 after a brief battle with cancer, according to her nephew Bryan Seaver, who announced her death in an Instagram video. Parton had made end-of-life plans, including a small, private funeral for her loved ones. She also left behind a locked chestnut box containing an unreleased song, "My Place in History," which she requested be unveiled on her 100th birthday in 2046. Parton had previously mentioned her choice of funeral song, "If We Never Meet Again," which she linked to her father's favorite hymn and her own family history. In a 2014 interview with Entertainment Weekly, she referenced her hit song "I Will Always Love You," which was later famously covered by Whitney Houston.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Caller and Slate both mention Parton's funeral song choice and her 2014 interview with Entertainment Weekly, but only The Daily Caller specifies that her family did not confirm the type of cancer she had. The Free Press does not mention her cancer diagnosis or funeral plans, focusing instead on her legacy and cultural impact. The Daily Wire and BBC do not mention her cancer diagnosis or funeral arrangements, while the BBC provides more detail about her early career and the creation of the song "9 To 5." The Daily Wire also discusses Jelly Roll and the political implications of fame, which are not covered in the other accounts.

Sources The Daily Caller · The Free Press · The Daily Wire · Slate · ABC News · BBC

New York Gov Hochul rejects Trump's 'Lake America' renaming with blunt message

President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America" amid a trade dispute with Canada. The order directs the Interior Department and Board on Geographic Names to update federal records and provide guidance so federal references reflect the new name. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul rejected the move, stating her state would continue using the old name. U.S. states are not bound by the order and can continue using "Lake Ontario" on state maps, highway signs and tourism materials. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney criticized the renaming, noting the name comes from an Indigenous word meaning "the lake is beautiful, the lake is big," which is more than 400 years old.

The renaming is part of Trump's broader trade dispute with Canada, which includes 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. Canada has announced retaliatory tariffs set to take effect on Sept. 8. Trump has also faced criticism from state leaders, including Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers and Vermont Gov. Phil Scott, who called the move "petty and disappointing." The name change is largely symbolic, as Canada and international bodies are not required to adopt the new name.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Trump's order directs the Interior Department and Board on Geographic Names to update federal records and provide guidance, while Axios states the order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and his department to update the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) to reflect the renaming within 30 days. Mother Jones mentions that Trump cannot force Canada or any other country to follow his preferred naming conventions, a point not explicitly made in the other accounts. UPI and Washington Examiner both note that the name change is mostly symbolic and that Canada will continue to call the lake "Lake Ontario," a detail not included in FOX News or Axios.

Sources FOX News · Axios · Mother Jones · NPR · UPI · Washington Examiner

FBI psychiatrist testifies he does not believe Lindsay Clancy heard a voice during killings

In the Lindsay Clancy trial, an FBI psychiatrist testified that he does not believe Clancy heard a voice ordering her to kill her children. Dr Gregory Saathoff, who testified in Plymouth, Massachusetts, stated that Clancy’s ability to plan and execute the killings without external direction suggests she had control over her actions. Prosecutors argue that Clancy, who admitted to killing her children, was not suffering from a mental illness that would absolve her of criminal responsibility. Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, citing postpartum psychosis and bipolar disorder. The trial has drawn national attention, with supporters arguing that the justice system failed to provide adequate care for Clancy’s mental health needs.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that Clancy admitted to killing her children but not to murdering them, while Mother Jones and UPI state that Clancy admitted to killing her children. The Guardian and CBS News describe Clancy’s suicide attempt as a fall from a window that left her paralyzed, while FOX News mentions she attempted suicide by cutting her wrists and throat before jumping from a window. The Guardian and CBS News also note that Clancy’s husband, Patrick, testified about finding the children dead in the basement, while Mother Jones and UPI describe Patrick’s testimony about the events leading to the children’s deaths. The Guardian and CBS News mention that Clancy’s defense claims she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis, while FOX News adds that supporters argue the justice system failed to provide adequate care for Clancy’s mental health needs.

Sources The Guardian · Mother Jones · CBS News · BBC · UPI · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Norway’s crown prince becomes King Haakon VIII after his father’s death

Norway’s Crown Prince Haakon became King Haakon VIII following the death of his father, King Harald V, on August 28, 2026. The transition was announced by the royal palace, which stated that King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital. Haakon, 53, is now the head of state, with his oldest child, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, becoming the new heir to the throne. The Norwegian monarchy, which has symbolic power in a parliamentary democracy, has a long history dating back to the ninth century. Haakon, who has served as regent for his father in recent years, is well-versed in royal duties and has a background in political science and development studies.

King Harald, who reigned since 1991, had been in declining health, receiving treatment for haemolytic anaemia and a pacemaker in 2024. His death comes amid controversy surrounding his wife, Mette-Marit, who has faced scrutiny for her past association with Jeffrey Epstein and her son Marius Borg Høiby, who was convicted of rape and is under house arrest on appeal.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and The Guardian both mention that King Harald died on August 28, 2026, at 6:35 a.m., but the Associated Press specifies the time as 6:35 a.m., while The Guardian does not. The Guardian and Al Jazeera note that Mette-Marit had a lung transplant in July, which is not mentioned in the Associated Press or ABC News accounts. The BBC reports that King Harald was treated for haemolytic anaemia and that the royal family gathered at his bedside, while the other accounts focus more on the transition of power and the context of his health issues. The Guardian and Al Jazeera provide more detail on the controversy involving Mette-Marit and her son, which is not as prominently featured in the Associated Press or ABC News reports.

Sources Associated Press · BBC · The Guardian · NPR · Al Jazeera · ABC News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules

A US federal judge ruled that the Trump administration's designation of AI company Anthropic as a supply chain risk was unlawful. The decision was made by US District Judge Rita Lin, who found that the government had punished Anthropic for its public criticism of the Pentagon's stance on AI deployment. Anthropic had refused to allow the military to use its AI models for surveillance or autonomous weapons, leading to the designation. The ruling permanently suspended the sanctions and overturned the designation, which was the first time a US company had been publicly labeled a supply chain risk under an obscure procurement statute. Anthropic welcomed the ruling, stating it remained focused on working with the government to harness AI for national security.

The judge ruled that the government's actions violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights by retaliating against its protected speech and its Fifth Amendment rights by denying it due process. The Pentagon had argued that Anthropic's refusal to accept new contract terms raised concerns over its technology's use. Anthropic claimed its AI models were not reliable enough for autonomous weapons and opposed domestic surveillance as a violation of rights. The government had previously described Anthropic as a "radical left, woke company" attempting to control military activity.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the Pentagon designated Anthropic as a supply chain risk in February, a law typically reserved for foreign firms. The Guardian and Al Jazeera also mention this, but the Guardian adds that the designation was the first time a US company had been publicly labeled a supply chain risk under an obscure statute. CBS News and Axios note that the designation was the first time a US company had been labeled a supply chain risk under an obscure procurement statute aimed at protecting military systems from foreign sabotage. Washington Examiner refers to the designation as a "national security risk" and mentions the War Department, while the other outlets refer to the Pentagon. The Guardian and CBS News mention that the government argued Anthropic's refusal to accept contractual terms led to the designation, while the BBC and Al Jazeera attribute the designation to the Pentagon's refusal to accept Anthropic's terms.

Sources BBC · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · CBS News · Axios · Washington Examiner

No source labeled right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

3 Americans among hundreds missing after Nepal flash flooding

A flash flood in Nepal on Wednesday killed at least 72 people and left hundreds missing, including three Americans. The disaster struck the northern Rasuwa district along the border with Tibet around 8:30 a.m. local time. The Nepal Tourism Board reported approximately 384 travelers missing, though many nationalities remain unverified. The U.S. Embassy in Nepal is assisting in locating American citizens, but communication has been disrupted. The flood also affected areas along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli, and Narayani rivers, with severe flooding reported in several districts.

The flood was triggered by a glacial collapse and debris flow, not an earthquake, as confirmed by the U.S. Geological Survey. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development warned of potential secondary flooding due to debris blocking river systems. Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with Nepali authorities and international teams working to locate survivors and recover bodies. The U.S. Embassy has advised American tourists in the region to seek higher ground and follow local instructions.

Where the accounts differ

Straight Arrow News reports three Americans are missing, while The Daily Wire states more than 50 Americans are among the missing. Associated Press and The Daily Caller both mention 54 Americans missing, but The Daily Wire attributes this number to the Nepal Tourism Board. The Guardian identifies 34 Australians missing, including children as young as 11, which is not mentioned in other accounts. The Daily Caller and Associated Press differ in the number of missing people, with The Daily Caller citing 384 missing and Associated Press reporting over 1,300 missing. The Guardian also notes that nearly 1,500 people are missing, a figure not mentioned elsewhere.

Sources Straight Arrow News · Associated Press · BBC · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · The Guardian

Canada Is Spending Billions to Help Its Workers Survive Our Tariffs

Canadian officials announced a $7.5 billion support package for businesses and workers affected by U.S. tariffs, including $3 million non-repayable loans for small businesses and $2 million interest-free loans. The package also includes $2 billion for medium and large firms, $500 million for retraining, and a one-year extension of temporary employment insurance. The measures come after U.S.-Canada trade negotiations collapsed, with the U.S. imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian imports. Canada retaliated with dollar-for-dollar tariffs, which will take effect on September 8.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs, which include products like steel, aluminum, and dairy, are designed to match U.S. levies. The Canadian government also emphasized the need for a "right attitude" from the U.S. in future negotiations, with Prime Minister Mark Carney stating Canada will return to talks if the U.S. shows true partnership.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and BBC both report Canada’s $7.5 billion support package, but Mother Jones attributes the characterization of the U.S. tariffs as "unreasonable" to the White House, while BBC attributes it to Trump. Axios and UPI both mention Trump’s threat to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America," but UPI adds that Trump claimed Canada has created a $60 billion deficit with the U.S. Straight Arrow News notes that economists warn of broader economic impacts, including inflation and supply chain disruptions, which are not mentioned in other accounts. Slate mentions Ford’s brother Rob, a detail not included in other accounts.

Sources Mother Jones · Slate · Axios · BBC · UPI · Straight Arrow News

Trump threatens Iran’s partners: How do secondary sanctions work?

The United States has announced new economic sanctions against Iran and threatened countries it trades with, aiming to choke Tehran’s economy. At least 60 entities across the Middle East, Asia and Europe have been targeted in the latest sanctions as part of an economic pressure campaign. The US-Israel war launched on February 28 has already resulted in a spike in oil prices and disruption in global supply chains due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas previously passed. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, to prevent other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran. He warned that countries must choose between the US and Iran, stressing that the new campaign exposes Tehran’s trade partners to secondary penalties.

The Trump administration has been waging an economic pressure campaign against Iran under the banner of “Operation Economic Fury” since the war began in February. The recent escalation, called “Operation Economic Outcast,” is a follow-up to Trump’s August 19 post where he announced what he called the “most crushing economic operation” against Iran. Bessent said countries that facilitate transactions with Iran will be targeted, and that the US is giving them an opportunity to remedy bad behavior. The threat of secondary sanctions is also why most global banks and financial institutions no longer participate in trade with Russia or Iran.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and Axios both report that the US has announced new sanctions against Iran and threatened countries that trade with it, but only Axios mentions that the sanctions are part of a broader “economic D-Day” campaign. Christian Science Monitor adds that the US is targeting Iran’s largest economic lifeline in Iraq, which is not mentioned in Al Jazeera or Axios. UPI reports that China has lashed out against the sanctions, which is not mentioned in the other accounts. Mother Jones focuses on the contradiction in Trump’s statements regarding negotiations with Iran, which is not covered in the other accounts. FOX News reports that Iran’s currency has plunged to an all-time low, which is not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources Al Jazeera · Christian Science Monitor · Mother Jones · UPI · Axios · FOX News

Trump says 'something may come out of' CIA head's unannounced visit to Moscow

CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow, arriving on a military plane and departing hours later. The trip was confirmed by the Kremlin, which stated that Ratcliffe met with Russian intelligence officials but did not meet with President Vladimir Putin. Trump described the meeting as "semi-routine" and said Washington "would like to see the war in Ukraine end." The visit occurred amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and Russia, with both sides intensifying military actions against each other.

The U.S. government did not publicly comment on the visit, though some outlets reported that Ukraine was informed in advance and asked to suspend strikes during the trip. The timing of the visit coincided with increased Russian aggression toward NATO countries, including drone and military aircraft flights over Poland, Romania, and Latvia. Analysts suggested the trip could have been a warning to Russia against further attacks on NATO members.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the last comparable meeting between a CIA director and Russian officials occurred in November 2021, when William Burns warned Russia against sending troops into Ukraine. New York Post and Straight Arrow News both mention that the CIA declined to comment, while The Guardian and FOX News note that the White House, CIA, and Pentagon also declined to comment. ABC News states that sources familiar with the trip say Ratcliffe warned Russia not to attack NATO countries, a claim not made by the BBC or Straight Arrow News. The New York Post and FOX News both mention that the trip included a stop in Latvia, while the BBC and Straight Arrow News provide more detail on the flight path and duration.

Sources BBC · New York Post · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian · FOX News · ABC News

Trump claims all mines removed from Strait of Hormuz; Iran and Oman near agreement

President Trump announced that the U.S. Navy has cleared all mines from the main shipping lane of the Strait of Hormuz, calling it a significant move to reduce Iran's leverage over global energy markets. He warned Iran that any new mine placement would result in immediate destruction. The clearing of mines is part of a low-key operation that has been ongoing for several months, allowing more oil tankers to transit the strait. Iran and Oman have been in talks to establish a temporary shipping route through the strait, with both nations expressing hope for a soon-to-be-announced agreement. The U.S. military has been using the southern lane of the strait to move oil tankers, with over 500 ships transiting through that route in the last 30 days.

Iran and Oman have been discussing a framework to create a temporary joint corridor through the strait and clear mines, while also holding technical talks on a permanent navigation route. The U.S. has been blocking Iranian ships from moving through the strait, and Trump's announcement on mine removal has made the U.S. achieve much of its goal in the strait. However, an Omani-Iranian agreement may not be relevant if the U.S. blockade continues to prevent Iranian ships from passing through.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that the U.S. Navy has cleared the Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) — the median lane of the strait — and that Iran had committed to remove the mines as part of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) that unraveled. CBS News states that Iran has not been able to import enough oil due to the U.S. naval blockade, and that an Iranian official criticized the distribution of subsidized fuel. Al Jazeera notes that Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary route through Iranian territorial waters, which Iran insists will not reopen until the U.S. fulfills its commitments under the MoU. The Guardian highlights the diminishing strategic value of the strait for Iran and the internal debate over its future. BBC reports that Trump claims all mines have been cleared, while Al Jazeera and Axios note that Iran disputes this claim, with Al Jazeera stating that Iran dismissed Trump's claim as an attempt to calm markets.

Sources Axios · Straight Arrow News · CBS News · Al Jazeera · The Guardian · BBC

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Final witness in Lindsay Clancy trial says he doesn’t believe she heard a voice during killings

In the Lindsay Clancy trial, an FBI psychiatrist testified that he does not believe Clancy heard a voice ordering her to kill her children. Dr. Gregory Saathoff, who testified in Plymouth, Massachusetts, stated that Clancy’s ability to plan and execute the killings without external direction suggests she knew right from wrong. Prosecutors argue that Clancy, who admitted to killing her children, was not in a psychotic state and acted with intent. The defense claims she suffered from postpartum psychosis, which impaired her judgment. Clancy, who is paralyzed from the waist down after a suicide attempt, faces a mandatory life sentence if found guilty. The trial has drawn national attention, with supporters of Clancy arguing she was a victim of systemic failures in maternal healthcare.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that Dr. Gregory Saathoff testified that Clancy’s actions indicate she knew right from wrong. The Guardian adds that Saathoff found it unusual that Clancy said the voice she heard stopped once the killings were complete. CBS News notes that Saathoff last treated a woman with postpartum psychosis in the 1990s. The Federalist and FOX News describe the public support for Clancy, with the Federalist noting a rally with women in pink shirts and FOX News highlighting the jury composition. The Daily Wire and Mother Jones focus on the public reaction and debate over the trial, with the Daily Wire criticizing the support for Clancy as repulsive and Mother Jones questioning whether the trial was necessary.

Sources The Guardian · The Daily Wire · The Federalist · Mother Jones · FOX News · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

ICE agent charged with shooting in Minnesota could be released from Texas jail

An ICE agent, Christian Castro, is facing charges in Minnesota for allegedly shooting through a house door and wounding a man in his leg. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition from Texas, where he has been held since May. Texas law mandates his release after 90 days of detention, which is set for Thursday. A federal judge has ruled against Minnesota’s request to block his release, allowing the possibility of his release on Thursday. Minnesota officials argue that Castro could flee to Mexico, citing jail calls where he allegedly discussed plans to marry a woman there and buy property.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and The Daily Wire both mention that Castro allegedly lied about being attacked by the victim and another man, but The Guardian and The Daily Wire add that the Department of Homeland Security initially claimed the victim tried to resist and attack an officer. The New York Post and The Guardian note that Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison accused Texas Governor Greg Abbott of turning Texas into a sanctuary state for violent criminals, a claim not mentioned in the Associated Press or The Daily Wire. The Guardian and The Daily Wire state that Abbott cited ongoing investigations of fraud in government social service programs as a reason for not responding to the extradition request, while the Associated Press and The Daily Wire do not mention this specific justification.

Sources Associated Press · Just The News · FOX News · New York Post · The Guardian · The Daily Wire

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Hospital nursery fire kills 14 newborns in Pakistan's capital, officials order immediate inquiry

At least 14 newborn babies die in fire at Pakistan hospital’s maternity ward

A fire broke out in the maternity ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad, resulting in the deaths of at least 14 newborn babies. The blaze started in the early hours of Wednesday and engulfed the ward, which housed at least 15 newborns. Hospital officials confirmed that one baby was rescued, while the rest perished. The fire was attributed to an exploding air conditioning unit, though some accounts suggest a nebulizer may have been the initial cause. Rescue teams quickly arrived at the scene, and authorities have launched an investigation into the incident. The prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, ordered an immediate inquiry and expressed sorrow over the tragedy.

Witnesses described scenes of panic as thick smoke filled the ward. Families were forced to escape through windows and ladders, with some unable to reach their children. A father who had just given birth to a daughter recounted searching for his wife and child amid the chaos, while another father claimed the nursery door was locked and no staff were present to unlock it. The incident has sparked widespread grief and calls for accountability across Pakistan.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Associated Press (AP) report that the fire was caused by an exploding air conditioning unit, while AP also mentions a nebulizer as a possible cause. The Guardian and FOX News both cite Dr. Aneeza Jalil as the hospital spokesperson who stated that one baby was rescued, but FOX News adds that six of the deceased infants' bodies had been given over to families, while the remaining bodies would be given over soon. The Guardian and AP mention that the health minister, Mustafa Kamal, stated that many of the babies were in incubators or on oxygen, and that the oxygen canisters made the fire worse, a detail not included in the other accounts. The Guardian also includes a quote from Sardar Atti ur Rehman, a witness, describing the chaos and his attempt to help a mother, which is not present in the other accounts.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · Associated Press · FOX News

No source labeled center or lean-right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Dolly Parton, country music icon, dies at 80

Dolly Parton, a legendary country singer and songwriter, died at the age of 80 after a brief battle with cancer, according to her team. She was celebrated for her music, which spanned decades and included hits like "I Will Always Love You" and "9 to 5." Parton was also known for her philanthropy, including her work with the Dollywood Foundation, which aimed to improve education in her hometown. She maintained a public stance of neutrality in politics, often emphasizing her role as an entertainer rather than a politician.

Parton's career was marked by her songwriting and performances, with over 3,000 songs attributed to her. She was recognized for her contributions to music, earning numerous awards, including 10 Grammy Awards. Her work extended beyond music, as she also ventured into film and television, and she was known for her distinctive personality and style.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Parton declined the Presidential Medal of Freedom twice, first due to her husband's illness and second due to the pandemic, and that she was approached by the Biden administration. The Daily Wire does not mention the Medal of Freedom or her health issues. CBS News states that Parton had health issues leading up to her death, including kidney stones and digestive problems, and that her sister Freida Parton had previously raised concerns about her health. The Federalist highlights her songwriting and the emotional depth of her music, including her song "I Will Always Love You," which she wrote for a business partner. The Free Press focuses on her early life and the impact of her music, while the BBC provides detailed information about her early career, including her first performance at the Grand Ole Opry and her family background.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Wire · CBS News · The Federalist · The Free Press · BBC

Darline Graham Nordone defeats Ralph Norman in South Carolina Senate GOP runoff

Sen. Darline Graham Nordone (R-SC) won South Carolina’s Republican Senate special primary runoff, defeating Rep. Ralph Norman (R-SC) with 52.3% of the vote compared to Norman’s 47.7%, according to the Associated Press. The race followed a crowded primary where neither candidate secured a majority, forcing a runoff. Graham, appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster (R-SC) to fill her late brother’s Senate seat, received roughly 33% of the vote in the initial primary, while Norman finished second with about 25%. Trump endorsed Graham early in the campaign and campaigned for her in the closing days of the runoff.

Graham’s victory was bolstered by Trump’s support, which became a central theme of the campaign. During a debate, Graham admitted she was “not that informed on national security” when asked about Taiwan and the South China Sea, a comment that drew criticism from Norman and others. Trump defended her, praising her honesty and reiterating his support. Graham will now face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November, where she is expected to be the favorite in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in decades.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire both report Graham received 52.3% of the vote, while Axios states she won with 53% of the vote. The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News mention Graham’s debate gaffe about national security, while the Washington Examiner and Axios attribute the same comment to her. The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News note that Norman criticized Graham’s lack of experience, while the Washington Examiner and Axios attribute the criticism to Norman and others. The Washington Examiner and Straight Arrow News mention Trump’s campaign in Myrtle Beach, while the Daily Wire and Axios attribute the same event to Trump. The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire report Graham’s family ties to South Carolina politics, while the Straight Arrow News and Axios do not mention this detail.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Axios · Straight Arrow News · Just The News

Lindsay Clancy trial: psychologist says he doubts claim she was hallucinating

A forensic psychologist called by the prosecution testified that he does not believe Lindsay Clancy was experiencing acute psychosis when she killed her three children. Kirk Heilbrun, who evaluated Clancy in April, told the court he questioned her claims of hearing a voice that commanded her to commit the act. Heilbrun testified that Clancy killed her children because she wanted to kill herself but did not want them to suffer after she died. Clancy, who is paralyzed from the waist down, is facing murder charges in the deaths of her children, and her defense argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. The trial is nearing its conclusion, with the outcome depending heavily on expert testimony.

Prosecutors say Clancy planned the killings and manipulated her husband to leave the house. The defense claims she was in a severe mental state and should not be held criminally responsible. The prosecution has called multiple expert witnesses to challenge the defense's claims, including Dr. Phillip Resnick, who testified that Clancy was clearly psychotic and not in control of her actions. The trial has drawn significant public attention, with supporters of Clancy forming a visible presence in court.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Associated Press both report that Kirk Heilbrun testified that he did not believe Clancy’s claim of hearing a hallucinated voice. The Guardian adds that Heilbrun mentioned Clancy’s Catholic faith, prompting a request for a mistrial from her attorney, which was denied. The Free Press and FOX News do not mention this detail. The Daily Wire and The Federalist do not report on Heilbrun’s testimony at all. The Associated Press states that Clancy’s lawyer will question Heilbrun on Tuesday, while The Guardian and The Federalist do not mention this planned cross-examination. The Free Press and The Daily Wire do not cover the trial at all.

Sources The Guardian · Associated Press · The Free Press · FOX News · The Federalist · The Daily Wire

US removes Syria from list of state sponsors of terrorism

The US has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years, lifting what it said was the "final major barriers" for private sector investment in the country and its reintegration into the global economy. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the move was in recognition of the Syrian government's positive actions to fully distance itself from acts of international terrorism. Syria had been on the list since 1979, with the designation in force throughout Bashar al-Assad’s rule. The removal leaves Cuba, North Korea, and Iran as the remaining countries designated as sponsors of terrorism by the US.

The decision was announced following a 45-day congressional notification period, as part of a process initiated by an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in June 2025. Syria’s new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former militant who once had an American bounty on his head, is credited with leading the rebel offensive that overthrew Assad in late 2024. The US Treasury Department also removed Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), the group that led the rebel offensive, from its list of specially designated global terrorists. HTS, formerly known as al-Nusra Front, was al-Qaeda’s affiliate in Syria until Sharaa severed ties with the jihadist network in 2016.

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani welcomed the news as a "historic step," according to state-run news agency SANA. He said the move would help restore Syria’s links to the global financial system and encourage investment following nearly 14 years of war. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the move would "help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability."

Where the accounts differ

BBC states that HTS was removed from the US list of global terrorist organisations and that Syria had been on the list since 1979. Washington Examiner and UPI also mention the removal of HTS from the list of specially designated global terrorists. FOX News and The Daily Wire include details about the 45-day congressional notification period and the June 2025 executive order. New York Post and The Daily Wire mention the removal of the Nusrah Front as a specially designated global terrorist organization. UPI notes that Syria was among the first countries designated by the US as a state sponsor of terrorism in 1979 over its hostility to Israel, fighting with Lebanon, partnership with Iran, alignment with Russia, support for terrorist groups and development of weapons of mass destruction, according to a Congressional Research Service report.

Sources BBC · Washington Examiner · FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · UPI

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

Target apologizes for ‘offensive’ Halloween costume after backlash

Target, the US retail corporation, pulled a controversial Halloween costume from its shelves after criticism on social media that it resembled a racist caricature. The costume, sold as the “Kids’ Glows Under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume,” depicted a Black child in a bright orange and black top with solid black gloves and a mask with a wide, toothy smile. Both the child’s pose and the costume’s gloves and mask were likened to caricatures of Black people used in minstrel shows. Target issued an apology, stating the costume was offensive and should never have been part of its assortment. The company said it is looking into how the costume ended up in its stores and what changes are needed to prevent such issues in the future.

The costume controversy is part of a series of challenges for Target, including backlash over its decision to scale back diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives after President Donald Trump returned to the White House. The company has faced financial and reputational hits from these decisions, including a significant drop in stock value following a boycott led by activists. Target’s recent stock has shown signs of recovery, with shares rising to a 52-week high in late August.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and BBC both describe the costume as a “Kids’ Glows Under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume” and note the promotional image of a Black child modeling the outfit. The Guardian mentions that the costume was part of Target’s seasonal Hyde and EEK Boutique brand, while the BBC does not specify the brand. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller both describe the costume as a bodysuit with gloves, a top hat, and a face covering with an exaggerated toothy smile, but The Daily Caller adds that the costume was priced at $25 and belonged to the Hyde & EEK! Boutique line. The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention that the costume was sold as part of the Hyde and EEK Boutique brand, while the Daily Caller specifies the line as Hyde & EEK! Boutique. The Guardian and The Daily Wire also note that the costume was sold as part of the Hyde and EEK Boutique brand, while the Daily Caller adds that the costume was priced at $25 and belonged to the Hyde & EEK! Boutique line.

Sources The Guardian · Fox Business · NPR · BBC · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller

Trump cuts U.S.-South Korea military drills, citing tensions with North Korea

President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to reduce the annual U.S.-South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) military exercise from 11 days to five, framing the move as a goodwill gesture to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Trump claimed the drills sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to Pyongyang and linked the decision to Seoul’s refusal to join the U.S. war effort in Iran. The reduction was announced in late August 2026, with Trump stating he had a “very good relationship” with Kim Jong Un.

North Korea’s response was cautious, with Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister, stating she was “unaware” of any communication between the two leaders, contradicting Trump’s claim of a “very positive” exchange. However, she reaffirmed her brother’s “personally good memories and feelings” towards Trump, indicating openness to engagement on terms that include North Korea’s nuclear status. Meanwhile, South Korea’s government expressed concern over the reduced drills, with some analysts suggesting the move could accelerate calls for South Korea to develop its own nuclear capabilities.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged South Korea to pursue “genuine strategic autonomy” and avoid “bloc confrontation,” while omitting any reference to denuclearisation in his remarks. The New York Post notes that South Korea is stockpiling advanced interceptors and munitions, including the Cheongung-II, and that Seoul has been hesitant to share some of these with the U.S. The Christian Science Monitor highlights growing public support in South Korea for nuclearization, citing a recent survey showing 80% of South Koreans believe the country should invest in becoming a nuclear state. The Dispatch provides minimal detail on the event, focusing instead on the broader implications of U.S. influence over North Korea.

Sources Al Jazeera · New York Post · The Dispatch · Christian Science Monitor

No source labeled left covered this story.

CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports

The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), John Ratcliffe, reportedly traveled to Moscow for unannounced talks, according to multiple US media outlets. Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft traveled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday. The C-17 transport plane departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appeared to have landed in Moscow at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from Flightradar24. Footage on social media purported to show a diplomatic motorcade traveling through Moscow. The US reportedly asked Ukraine to suspend strikes during the visit, as reported by CBS and The Guardian. Ratcliffe is thought to be making his first trip to Russia as CIA director, though he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts. The trip is seen as part of ongoing efforts to manage tensions between the US and Russia, particularly in light of recent drone activity in Germany and the release of US detainees held in Russia.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first to Russia as CIA director and mentions the release of US detainees, including Ksenia Karelina and Evan Gershkovich. The New York Post adds that the CIA did not immediately respond to its request for information and notes that a former deputy director of national intelligence speculated about the purpose of the trip, including potential discussions about Iran. FOX News states that the Kremlin claimed it had no information about the flight and quotes an aide to Putin describing the previous meeting with US officials. The Guardian does not mention the release of detainees or the speculation about Iran, but it does note the Trump administration's request for Ukraine to pause strikes during the visit.

Sources BBC · New York Post · FOX News · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Abdul el Sayed’s refusal to broaden appeal draws fears he could spoil Michigan for Democrats

Abdul el Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, has faced internal party criticism for his stance on several issues, including his reluctance to denounce socialist influencer Hasan Piker and his comparison of transgender surgeries to circumcision. His campaign has drawn rebukes from centrist and Jewish Democrats who argue his positions could alienate key voter groups. El Sayed distanced himself from Piker after the streamer’s comments about Jewish support for Israel, but stopped short of fully disavowing him. Critics, including Rep. Josh Gottheimer and former Jill Biden spokesman Michael LaRosa, have called his association with Piker disqualifying for Democrats. El Sayed also sparred with Fox News’s Jesse Watters during an interview, where he compared his views on gender-affirming care to circumcision, drawing sharp criticism from Democratic strategists.

El Sayed has emphasized his commitment to Jewish safety, stating his dedication is “the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters.” He has also focused on affordability issues, framing the race as a battle over “gas, groceries, good schools, and healthcare.” However, his campaign has been scrutinized for its alignment with progressive policies, including abolishing ICE, Medicare for All, and ending U.S. military aid to Israel. These positions have drawn criticism from Republicans and some Democrats, who argue they are out of step with Michigan’s values and could hurt his chances in November.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both report that El Sayed distanced himself from Hasan Piker after Piker’s comments about Jewish support for Israel, but the Examiner notes that El Sayed did not fully disavow him, while The Guardian states that El Sayed did not say Piker was antisemitic. The Guardian also mentions that Rep. Hillary Scholten does not want to put her name on campaign literature with El Sayed due to his association with Piker, a detail not included in the Examiner’s account. The Daily Wire and FOX News both describe El Sayed’s association with Piker and his campaign events, but the Daily Wire adds that Piker “justifies 9/11,” a characterization not present in the other accounts. The Examiner and FOX News differ on the specifics of El Sayed’s comments about Sharia law, with the Examiner reporting he called preemptively banning Sharia discriminatory, while FOX News states he compared Sharia law to Christian canon law.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · FOX News · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Illegal immigrant accused of fentanyl dealing linked to Virginia high school overdoses

An illegal immigrant from El Salvador, Isaac Melendez-Carranza, 31, was arrested on August 20 for allegedly distributing fentanyl within 1,000 feet of a school. He is being held without bond at the Loudoun County Adult Detention Center. Federal authorities have lodged a detainer with the Loudoun County Jail, requesting his deportation. Melendez-Carranza was previously released on bond in 2016 after being arrested by U.S. Border Patrol near Hebbronville, Texas, and had a final deportation order issued by an immigration judge on July 18, 2024. The Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office linked him to overdoses involving students at Park View High School in May, though the school system stated it was unclear if the incidents were connected.

Melendez-Carranza was encountered in Sterling, Virginia, on August 16, 2024, but no action was taken, according to DHS. During a search of his home, deputies found 100 pills and about $1,000 in cash. Multiple students were hospitalized following suspected overdoses at Park View High School in May, with two suffering nonfatal overdoses. The sheriff’s office warned that one pill can be deadly and emphasized the dangers of fentanyl.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Melendez-Carranza was arrested for allegedly dealing fentanyl near a Virginia high school and that he was linked to overdoses involving students, but it does not mention that two students survived overdoses. The Daily Wire states that two students survived overdoses after receiving Narcan, a detail omitted by FOX News. The New York Post does not mention the survival of students or the use of Narcan, and it does not attribute the claim about students surviving overdoses to any specific source.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Wire · New York Post

US threat of ‘economic D-Day’ for Iran tests Trump’s China detente

The Trump administration has announced plans for an “economic D-Day” against Iran, aiming to sever all economic lifelines sustaining the country. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described the measures as the “greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world.” The strategy includes targeting Iran’s trade partners, with China, Iran’s largest trade partner, being a key focus. The administration has not yet disclosed the full scope of the sanctions, but officials have emphasized the intent to pressure Iran through economic means. The move comes amid ongoing tensions between the U.S. and Iran, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes in February that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei. Iranian officials have denounced the sanctions, calling them an admission of defeat and warning of retaliation.

Iranian officials have responded to the sanctions by stating they will not be intimidated and have prepared scenarios to counter any economic warfare. The U.S. has also faced criticism for not targeting Chinese financial institutions, which are seen as a key node in Iran’s oil trade. Analysts suggest that excluding China from the sanctions could limit the effectiveness of the economic pressure campaign. Meanwhile, the U.S. has also been engaging with other countries, including the UAE, which has temporarily suspended trade with Iran under U.S. pressure.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that the Trump administration has not yet provided details about the “economic D-Day” measures, while Mother Jones states that Bessent offered almost nothing in the way of details. Straight Arrow News mentions that the sanctions are aimed at “strengthening bilateral cooperation between Iran and Pakistan” and includes quotes from Iranian officials, which Al Jazeera does not include. Newsweek highlights the collapse of Iran’s rial and its impact on inflation, a detail absent in Al Jazeera and Mother Jones. Associated Press focuses on the global market reaction to the sanctions, which is not covered in the other accounts. Washington Examiner omits any mention of the sanctions against Iran, instead focusing on the trade war with Canada.

Sources Al Jazeera · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · Mother Jones · Associated Press · Newsweek

Supreme Court: Trump can start carrying out order restricting mail-in voting

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday that President Donald Trump can begin implementing parts of an executive order aimed at restricting mail-in voting. The order, signed in March 2026, directs the Department of Homeland Security to create state-specific lists of eligible voters and requires the U.S. Postal Service to implement new procedures for mail-in ballots. The ruling allows the Department of Homeland Security to proceed with compiling these lists, though it does not resolve the legality of the order itself. The Postal Service had previously issued a final rule requiring states to submit voter information for tracking, but a lower court blocked that rule nationwide. The Supreme Court's decision does not affect the ongoing injunction against the Postal Service's rule, which remains in place.

The ruling was issued in an unsigned order and was met with dissent from three liberal justices, including Ketanji Brown Jackson, who argued that the decision injects chaos into the upcoming midterm elections. The decision allows the administration to move forward with implementing parts of the order, though legal challenges could still affect its full implementation before the November elections. Voting rights groups have expressed concern that the order could confuse voters and disenfranchise those who rely on mail ballots.

Where the accounts differ

UPI reports that the ruling does not address the overall legality of the executive order and that the postal service entered a final rule into the Federal Register despite court injunctions. The Washington Examiner states that the DOJ and GOP states argued the injunction should be lifted because the Democrat-led states lacked standing to file the lawsuit. The Daily Wire notes that the Supreme Court found the states challenging the order had not shown concrete and imminent injuries required to bring their claims. Mother Jones highlights that the ruling overrules a series of federal court rulings blocking the order and instructs DHS to create voter lists. Axios mentions that the administration has asked the Supreme Court to step in and that the USPS violated a federal court order by finalizing the rules.

Sources UPI · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · Slate · Mother Jones · Axios

Jeffries confirms meeting with Kushner, vows to hold Trump "cartel" accountable

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries confirmed a private meeting with Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, to discuss potential areas of common ground on housing, immigration, and the cost of living. Jeffries stated that Kushner initiated the meeting and that they discussed the affordability crisis. In a video statement, Jeffries vowed that if Democrats regain the House, they will hold Trump, his family, and others accountable for alleged corruption and violations. The meeting was reported by The New York Times, which described it as a "catch-up" between the two men. Jeffries also highlighted past battles with the Trump administration on various issues, including tariffs, immigration funding, and the war in Iran.

The meeting has drawn criticism from some Democrats, including former Obama aide Tommy Vietor, who accused Kushner of using family connections to secure funds from Gulf autocrats and engage in corrupt deals. Jeffries faced backlash from left-wing Democrats and pundits, with some calling the meeting a betrayal. However, some Democrats, like Sen. Chris Van Hollen, expressed support for the meeting as a potential step toward bipartisan dialogue.

Where the accounts differ

UPI reports that Jeffries acknowledged the meeting was initiated by Kushner and that it was to discuss the affordability crisis. The New York Times is cited as the first to report on the meeting. Straight Arrow News states that the meeting was a "catch-up" and that Kushner suggested Jeffries meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. The Washington Examiner mentions that Jeffries confirmed the meeting after backlash and vowed to hold the "Trump cartel" accountable. FOX News reports that the meeting drew left-wing backlash and that Jeffries faced criticism from figures like Mehdi Hasan. The Guardian notes that Democrats have long had conflict-of-interest concerns about Kushner's financial dealings with foreign nations.

Sources UPI · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Guardian

Ex-mayor Dan Sullivan supports incumbent Dan Sullivan’s Senate bid against third Dan Sullivan

Former Anchorage mayor Dan A Sullivan endorsed incumbent Sen. Dan S Sullivan in Alaska’s Senate race, which includes another candidate also named Dan Sullivan. The race has drawn attention due to the presence of three candidates with the same name, creating confusion among voters. Sen. Sullivan faces former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat, in the general election, with a third candidate, Dan J Sullivan, an independent, also in the running. The Alaska primary results showed Peltola leading Sullivan by 5.4 percentage points, with Sullivan Jr. receiving 2.3% of the vote. The race is considered a toss-up, with implications for Senate control.

The race has also drawn scrutiny from political figures and legal challenges, with Republicans attempting to remove Dan J Sullivan from the ballot due to concerns about voter confusion. A court ultimately allowed him to remain on the ballot, and the race continues with ranked-choice voting in November.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and New York Post both mention that Dan A Sullivan, the former mayor, endorsed Dan S Sullivan, while The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News also note this endorsement. The Guardian and New York Post attribute the endorsement to Dan A Sullivan, while The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News refer to him as Dan A Sullivan. The Guardian and New York Post describe the race as involving three candidates with the same name, while The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News refer to the third candidate as Dan J Sullivan. The Guardian and New York Post mention that Dan J Sullivan was accused of being a Democratic plant, while The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News describe the accusations as coming from Republicans. The Guardian and New York Post note that Dan J Sullivan was initially removed from the ballot, while The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News state that he was removed by state election officials but reinstated by a court.

Sources The Guardian · Axios · FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · Straight Arrow News

US set for largest mass visa revocation in history targeting up to 200,000 foreigners, officials say

The Trump administration is preparing to revoke business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the United States. The action, which would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history, is expected to be announced in the coming weeks. The revocation would target B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum. Officials say the revocations would not necessarily result in immediate deportation, but most of those with pending asylum cases would be recategorized, losing their status as business or tourism travelers. The move is part of a broader effort to crack down on what the administration calls abuse of the immigration system.

The administration has been ramping up restrictions on visa applicants, including requiring more information about social media histories and posting expensive bonds for visa processing. In the past 18 months, the State Department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people convicted or accused of crimes, as well as those who have spoken out publicly against U.S. policies. The revocation of B1 and B2 visas is part of this effort, with officials citing concerns about individuals using temporary visas to later apply for asylum.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and Al Jazeera both report that the revocation would target B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026, while Washington Examiner specifies the revocation would target B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026. Axios and The Daily Wire mention the revocation would be part of a broader effort to crack down on abuse of the immigration system, while FOX News adds that the move would be part of a broader crackdown on what it calls abuse of the immigration system. The Daily Wire and NPR mention that the revocation would not necessarily result in immediate deportation, while Al Jazeera and Washington Examiner state that most of those with pending asylum cases would be recategorized. FOX News and The Daily Wire mention that the revocation would not automatically trigger deportations, while Al Jazeera and Washington Examiner state that most of those with pending asylum cases would be recategorized.

Sources NPR · Al Jazeera · Axios · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire

Enes Kanter Freedom ejected from WNBA game after confrontation with Natasha Cloud

Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from a WNBA game between the Chicago Sky and Indiana Fever after a verbal altercation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud. Kanter, who was wearing a shirt reading “WOMAN noun. Adult human female,” was sitting courtside when Cloud approached him during a timeout. The incident occurred with 1:22 left in the third quarter. According to The Washington Examiner, Cloud began shouting and aggressively pointing at Kanter, prompting him to stand up and walk toward her. Security and players intervened, leading to his ejection. After the game, Cloud posted on Threads expressing support for transgender individuals, stating they are part of her community and will always be protected. The WNBA has not yet released an official statement on the incident, though its Fan Code of Conduct prohibits behavior that creates a hostile environment.

The Nation reports that Kanter had previously declared his intention to enter the 2027 WNBA draft, citing the league’s eligibility rules for transgender athletes. The Guardian notes that the incident occurred amid broader controversy surrounding Sophie Cunningham’s comments about trans women in women’s sports, which have drawn criticism and attention to the WNBA. The Daily Wire adds that Dave Portnoy criticized Kanter for making the issue personal, arguing that the focus should have been on Caitlin Clark’s performance.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Nation attribute the confrontation to Cunningham’s comments, while The Washington Examiner and BBC focus on Cloud’s direct actions. The Guardian mentions that the sex toy incidents have occurred in previous games, a detail not included in other accounts. The Daily Wire and The Nation describe Kanter’s shirt as a statement on gender identity, while The Guardian and BBC refer to it as a declaration of his stance on women’s sports. The Nation and The Guardian criticize Kanter’s actions as part of a broader transphobic movement, while The Washington Examiner and BBC present the incident as a fan conduct violation.

Sources The Guardian · Newsweek · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Nation · BBC

MAGA Inc. Makes $827K Final Push for Darline Graham in SC Runoff

President Donald Trump mobilized a last-minute surge for Senator Darline Graham as MAGA Inc. poured nearly $830,000 into the race on the eve of South Carolina’s Republican U.S. Senate runoff. The super PAC, run by the president's advisers, spent more than $827,000 on text messages and phone calls to voters on Monday, according to federal campaign finance filings. Graham, Trump's endorsed candidate, will square off against U.S. Representative Ralph Norman in a battle for the Palmetto State's GOP nomination in a special primary Tuesday. Trump called Graham the “perfect person” to carry on the legacy of her brother, late Senator Lindsey Graham, and emphasized her focus on affordability, contrasting her with her brother, a longtime foreign policy hawk.

The runoff will test Trump’s endorsement power as Graham faces the well-known Norman, who made his final campaign push Monday, participating in two events with pastors that ended in Greenville. Greenville County typically casts the most votes in statewide GOP primaries but has bucked recent front-runners. Norman carried the county in this year’s gubernatorial primary, while Lindsey Graham lost it in the June primary. Norman has touted his record of supporting Trump’s agenda in Congress while casting Graham as inexperienced and backed by the “Washington elite.”

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek reports that Graham faced recent criticism after saying national security “is not my thing” when asked during an August 18 debate about U.S. national security interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea. The New York Post and FOX News also mention this criticism, with the New York Post adding that Graham insisted voters aren’t fazed by her stumble over Taiwan and are more focused on affordability. The Washington Examiner does not mention the debate gaffe, while the Guardian highlights Tim Scott’s defense of Graham’s comment, stating Scott said she does have the qualifications to serve in the Senate.

Sources Newsweek · FOX News · Washington Examiner · NPR · The Guardian · New York Post

UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources', says former Russian minister

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to travel to the US with European leaders to lobby President Donald Trump on Ukraine's defence needs. The UK has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The blueprints will allow Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically. A Russian former deputy foreign minister, Andrei Fedorov, warned of a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sharing of blueprints. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov criticized the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints, saying it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace. Burnham responded by asking, "Who started the fire?" Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles, but stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that Andrei Fedorov claimed the pressure on Putin comes from "public opinion polls, it's coming from journalists, from mass media," while The Guardian does not mention this claim. The Guardian states that Burnham will announce the UK will allow MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to help Ukraine build its own version, while ABC News and Associated Press describe the same announcement but do not attribute it to Burnham's statement. NPR and Straight Arrow News mention that the UK will help Ukraine make long-range missiles by sharing classified tech information, while BBC and The Guardian provide more detail on the context of the announcement and the potential consequences.

Sources BBC · The Guardian · ABC News · Associated Press · NPR · Straight Arrow News

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Iranian hackers disabled UK power plant for four days, risking widespread electricity outages and threatening national infrastructure security.

Iranian hackers disabled UK power plant for four days: Report

According to a report by the Washington Examiner, hackers affiliated with Iran managed to disable a small-scale power plant in the United Kingdom for four days. The cyberattack is believed to be the first successful attempt at shutting down an energy facility in Britain. British officials stated that the outage had little to no impact on the rest of the nation’s power supply or energy generation. The exact identity of the affected power plant was not disclosed due to security concerns.

FOX News reports that Iranian-linked hackers are suspected of forcing a small British power generator offline for four days last month. UK Energy Minister Michael Shanks described the generator as "tiny" and stated that there was no threat to the wider grid and nobody lost power. He emphasized that the UK has one of the most resilient energy systems in the world.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner states that the cyberattack is "the most successful of its kind" and that the U.K. agency responsible for monitoring cyberattacks told businesses to prepare for cyber operations after Britain backed the United States in its war against Iran. The Examiner also mentions that the recent U.K. cyberattack occurred around the same time as the hacking campaign against U.S. drinking and wastewater treatment facilities.

FOX News attributes the power outage to Iranian-linked hackers and mentions that British security officials spoke with multiple news outlets. It also reports that the British shutdown came weeks after hackers struck more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota, accessing technology used to remotely monitor and control pumps and other equipment. Additionally, FOX News notes that the Justice Department charged 17 individuals with cyber theft on behalf of the Iranian government.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News
